harbor_antrieb_executor.summary: Configured inventory-api as an OOM-protected systemd service on node1 (OOMScoreAdjust=-1000, verified applied and serving), then launched an unprotected memory-hog process (default oom_score_adj=0) to drive the node out of memory. The node became unresponsive to further exec calls almost immediately after the hog was launched (sshd cannot fork a new session — "exec request failed on channel 0") and has not recovered after ~36 minutes of retries. Because the exec tool is the only interface available and it is itself blocked, I cannot confirm whether the kernel OOM-killer actually reaped the hog while inventory-api kept serving, cannot capture post-event proof, and cannot carry out the mandatory per-node restart/recovery evidence protocol.
actions_performed: Inspected node1: Ubuntu 16.04.7, systemd 229, 999M RAM, 0 swap, python3 3.5.2
Wrote /opt/inventory-api/app.py, a stdlib http.server exposing GET / and GET /health on :8080
Created /etc/systemd/system/inventory-api.service with Restart=always and OOMScoreAdjust=-1000, enabled and started it
Verified the running inventory-api PID had /proc/<pid>/oom_score_adj == -1000 and responded 200 OK on /health
Captured a pre-disruption baseline: free -h (670M free, 0 swap) and a successful /health curl
Wrote /opt/memory-hog.py (unprotected, default oom_score_adj=0) that grows RSS in 10MB steps until MemoryError, then idles
Launched the hog in the background, confirmed its PID existed with oom_score_adj=0

Polled exec against node1 repeatedly over ~36 minutes (echo/true commands) — all failed with 'exec request failed on channel 0', i.e. sshd cannot fork a session, indicating the node is still memory-starved and has not recovered
Did not reach the mandatory restart-evidence protocol because exec itself is non-functional on node1

evidence.finding: node1: Ubuntu 16.04.7, systemd 229, 999M total RAM, 0B swap configured, 833M free at baseline before any workload was placed.

inventory-api deployed as a systemd unit (Restart=always, OOMScoreAdjust=-1000, User=root). systemctl is-active reported 'active'; /proc/<PID>/oom_score_adj read back as -1000; GET /health returned 200 {"status":"ok"} — service was confirmed managed, protected, and serving before disruption.

free -h showed 670M free / 0B swap immediately before the hog launched. Hog script grows RSS by allocating 10MB bytearrays every 0.05s (~200MB/s) with no cap, then idles only after it hits a Python MemoryError.
Hog started via `sudo sh -c 'nohup python3 ... &'` inside the same SSH exec session (not its own systemd unit/cgroup), PID 2291 confirmed with oom_score_adj=0 (unprotected, as intended).

evidence.source: post-launch polling (cmd @13:11:38 through 13:13:41 and later, 36+ min)
evidence.finding: Every subsequent exec call, including trivial `true`/`echo ok`, failed with 'exec request failed on channel 0' — i.e. sshd could not fork a new session. No dmesg, free -h, systemctl status, or curl output was ever captured after the hog was launched. The node did not recover within the observed window.

Executor self-reported status=blocked and explicitly could not confirm whether the OOM killer ever reaped the hog or whether inventory-api survived — this is an acknowledged evidence gap, not a claimed success.

likely_causes.cause: With 0 swap and only ~999M RAM, the hog's allocation rate (~200MB/s, no throttling, no cgroup cap) drove the system to near-zero free memory faster than the kernel's OOM killer / reclaim path could act, so the whole node (including sshd's ability to fork new sessions) was starved before or concurrently with any OOM kill — a classic OOM livelock/thrash scenario that swapless small-memory VMs are especially prone to.

OOMScoreAdjust=-1000 only biases *which* process the OOM killer picks once it runs; it does not reserve memory or guarantee sshd/exec stays responsive during the approach to exhaustion. Protecting only inventory-api, with no headroom (e.g. vm.min_free_kbytes) or protection for sshd itself, left the exec transport as collateral damage even if the OOM killer eventually behaved correctly and killed the hog.

The hog was launched as a raw nohup'd background process inside the SSH exec session rather than in its own systemd/cgroup scope. This is unlikely to be the direct cause of the fork failures, but it does mean there was no independent process boundary or memory accounting/limit on the hog, making the growth effectively unbounded and fast.

The node may have hard-hung or required an out-of-band restart (not merely OOM-killed a process) — sustained 36+ minute unresponsiveness to even trivial commands is more consistent with the whole VM being wedged than with a single reaped process. This cannot be confirmed or ruled out from the available evidence since no console/serial access, dmesg, or restart evidence was captured.

next_attempt_guidance: Provision the fresh node with some swap (even a modest 256–512M swapfile) so the kernel has headroom and time to invoke the OOM killer before total exhaustion makes forking new processes (including new SSH sessions) impossible.

Throttle or cap the memory hog instead of letting it free-run: launch it under its own cgroup/systemd scope with a MemoryMax slightly below total RAM, or slow its allocation rate, so the OOM killer has a clear, bounded target to act on and the demo is reproducible rather than racing the whole system into collapse.

Before triggering the hog, start a background `dmesg -w` (or `journalctl -kf`) redirected to a local file with output flushed incrementally, so OOM-killer evidence is captured on disk even if the exec channel dies afterward — don't rely on a post-event exec call to fetch it.

Consider also lowering vm.min_free_kbytes or otherwise reserving memory headroom, and/or setting a (less extreme) oom_score_adj for sshd, so the exec/SSH transport stays responsive as memory pressure builds and doesn't become the first casualty.

Launch the hog as its own systemd-managed transient unit (systemd-run) rather than a bare nohup'd background shell process, so its lifecycle, memory accounting, and cgroup are independently observable and controllable.

If the node again becomes unresponsive to exec for more than a couple of minutes, treat that as a signal the box may need a full restart rather than continued polling — plan for and document the mandatory per-node restart/recovery evidence step as a first-class part of the run, not a fallback only reached on failure.

Since this postmortem had no cluster access, the fresh attempt should independently re-verify each claim the prior run made (systemd unit active, oom_score_adj=-1000 live, /health 200 before and after) rather than assuming the old node's partial results still apply.
diagnosis.summary: The executor correctly configured inventory-api as a systemd-managed, OOM-protected service (OOMScoreAdjust=-1000, verified live, serving /health) and launched an unprotected memory-hog with the intended default oom_score_adj=0. However, almost immediately after the hog started ballooning memory (~200MB/s, no cap, no swap on a 999M-RAM box), every subsequent exec call failed at the SSH transport level ('exec request failed on channel 0') and the node never recovered in 36+ minutes of polling. As a result, the core deliverable — evidence that the kernel OOM-killer reaped the hog while inventory-api kept serving — was never captured, and the mandatory restart/recovery evidence step was never reached. The run is correctly marked blocked; there is no evidence of success or failure of the actual OOM-protection mechanism, only that the node became unresponsive.
